problem: Object-based semantic SLAM maps contain only static landmarks (furniture), so movable objects such as keys, glasses or a remote are absent from the map. Prior object-goal navigation learns from raw pixels with millions of episodes, or uses a GCN only as a feature extractor, and neither exploits the explicit graph map to find unmapped objects.
motivation: Domestic robots must find misplaced small objects. Such objects are not placed randomly but appear near a few related static objects, so a hidden probabilistic model governs where they are. The paper asks whether a policy can learn this model directly on the compact graph map, sample-efficiently and with generalisation to unseen objects and environments.
key_idea: Use a graph convolutional network directly as the policy network on a semantic SLAM graph, with FastText word vectors as node features, outputting a distribution over pose nodes as navigation goals, trained with REINFORCE.
insight: Word-vector node features let the policy transfer to unseen target classes when they are semantically close to trained ones; the cellphone class, with no similar training class, is the failure case. Proxy-task pre-training (predicting which pose nodes are connected to a class) speeds learning and improves generalisation, from 0.92 to 0.96 success on unseen environments and from 0.72 to 0.76 on unseen classes. The learned policy is layout-independent because it learns the constant object co-occurrence structure rather than the specific probabilities.
method: Graph map G: pose nodes plus static landmark nodes (class label). Pose-pose edges mean traversable; landmark-pose edges mean in interaction range. Built from an object-based SLAM output.
Node features: 300-d FastText word vector for each landmark class and the target class; pose nodes are initialised to zero.

Policy network: one Kipf-Welling GCN layer (300→64, ReLU) followed by 3 FC layers (128→64→32→1) applied per node on concat(z_i, z_target). The output is logits over nodes, with landmark nodes masked to -100.

Training: REINFORCE with Adam at lr 1e-4. The agent gets reward if it finds the target within 10 goal selections. Goals are assumed always reachable, with no path-length cost. 10 agents × 20 random probabilistic models × 50,000 episodes.

Synthetic dataset: 1000-node pose graph with 4 room types (95% chance to keep the previous room type); 100-500 landmarks from 20 static classes; targets spawn near specific map objects with probabilities drawn from U(0.1, 0.9).
Proxy-task pre-training: on random maps with a different placement model, a binary cross-entropy classification of which pose nodes are connected to an instance of a given class.
Baselines: random policy (no repeats) and oracle policy (knows the hidden probabilities, picks the max-probability node first).

setting.backbone: 1-layer GCN + 3-layer MLP policy with frozen FastText word vectors (trained from scratch with REINFORCE, optional proxy pre-training)
setting.model_size: small (~ tens of thousands of parameters; GCN 300×64 + FC 128-64-32-1)
setting.training_data: Synthetic randomly generated graph maps and target placements (50,000 episodes per agent, 200 agents); FastText wiki-news-300d-1M pre-trained vectors; optional proxy-task pre-training on random maps
setting.observation: Symbolic graph-based semantic map (pose nodes and static object landmark nodes with class labels); no images
setting.action_space: High-level choice of a pose node in the graph as the next goal (max 10 goals per episode); reachability assumed
setting.simulator: Custom synthetic graph simulation (no physics simulator)
setting.privileged: Assumes a perfect object-based semantic map, perfect localisation and always-reachable goals; the object landmark classes are given correctly

numbers.extra: Trained on 20 random probabilistic models; evaluated on new maps and models; 10 goal budget; goals always reachable

numbers_note: Custom synthetic benchmark, not a standard one; SR converted from fractions to percent. Baselines (random 0.26, oracle 0.99 on unseen environments) are excluded per the rules. Steps is the paper's 'steps to target'.
results: On synthetic graph maps the GCN policy reaches 0.99 SR in training environments, matching the oracle (0.99 SR, 1.66 steps), versus 0.33 for random. In unseen environments it drops only to 0.96 SR (oracle 0.99). On unseen target classes it gets 0.76 SR (oracle 0.97, random 0.25). Pre-training speeds up learning and improves generalisation.
limitations: Evaluated only on synthetic, hand-designed graph maps with an assumed placement model. There is no real robot or real SLAM output, and future work is required for that.
Assumes perfect semantic maps, localisation and always-reachable goals; travel distance is ignored. Generalisation relies on the co-occurrence structure being constant across environments.
No study of hyperparameters, architecture or word-vector choice; unseen classes with no semantic neighbour (cellphone) fail.
